curriculum.title: God Promises to Put Things Right

core.big_idea: God responded to rebellion with both judgment and the promise of rescue.

passages.reading_note: Read the judgment against the serpent and introduce the promise in simple language.
Use only as a later canonical connection that evil will not win forever.

core.metanarrative_position: Promise: immediately after rebellion, God announces judgment on evil and the beginning of a rescue hope.

claims.statement: God pronounced judgment on the serpent after the rebellion.
Genesis 3:15 describes continuing conflict and a future crushing of the serpent.
Within the whole biblical story, Christians understand this promise as part of the hope fulfilled through Christ’s victory over evil.
Genesis 3:15 begins a rescue thread but does not by itself explain every later detail of the gospel.
claims.credible_alternative: Some interpreters treat the verse mainly as an explanation of human hostility toward serpents rather than a direct messianic prophecy.
claims.interpretive_hinge: Whether the verse is read only in its immediate narrative setting or also within later canonical patterns of conflict and victory.
claims.prohibited_overstatement: Do not claim that every element of the gospel is explicitly stated in this single verse.

core.interpretation_skill: Notice promise language; distinguish what Genesis 3:15 states from the later canonical connection to Christ.

learning.foundation_objective: Say that God judged evil and promised that evil would not win forever.
learning.extension_objective: Explain the difference between the words in Genesis 3:15 and the wider Christian connection to Jesus.
know: God did not ignore the rebellion.
God announced a future defeat of evil.
understand: God’s rescue plan begins while the damage of sin is still visible.
Later Scripture helps Christians see the promise within Christ’s victory.
practise: Thank God that evil does not have the final word.
Wait with hope when a good ending is not immediate.
become: A child who takes wrongdoing seriously while trusting God’s promised rescue.
success_evidence: The child states both judgment and promise.
The child avoids saying the verse names Jesus directly.
The child names hope as a fitting response.

zero_prep_card.objective: Children say that God judged evil and promised rescue.
zero_prep_card.opening: Show a knotted cord and ask: When something is badly tangled, does that mean it can never be put right?
say: God did not pretend the rebellion did not matter.
God judged the serpent and announced that the serpent would be defeated.
The Bible’s rescue story begins here and grows clearer over time.
Christians see this hope fulfilled through Jesus, but Genesis 3:15 is only the beginning of the explanation.
ask: Who receives judgment in these verses?
What future conflict does God describe?
Does evil win forever in God’s story?
How can hope change the way we face a hard situation?
zero_prep_card.do: Use the Promise Thread Card to connect Genesis 3:15 to later rescue passages without claiming they all say the same amount.
zero_prep_card.close: Pray: God, thank You that evil will not win forever. Help us trust Your rescue and wait with hope.

preparation.passage_context: Genesis 3:14-15 is part of God’s judgments after the first rebellion. The verse contains conflict, injury, and a future crushing of the serpent.
text_observations: The speech is addressed to the serpent.
The language includes conflict between the serpent’s offspring and the woman’s offspring.
One side is wounded; the serpent is crushed.
interpretation_notes: Teach the immediate text before the Christian canonical synthesis.
For Kids, “evil will not win forever” is clearer than technical language such as protoevangelium.
Keep judgment and promise together; hope is not denial of wrongdoing.
theological_guardrails: Do not say Genesis 3:15 explicitly narrates the cross or names Jesus.
Do not imply that God’s promise removes all present pain immediately.
Do not use frightening serpent imagery or graphic descriptions.

likely_questions.question: Is this verse about Jesus?
likely_questions.purpose: Answer: Christians see it as the beginning of a promise thread fulfilled in Jesus, though the verse itself does not give every detail.

likely_questions.question: Why did God not fix everything immediately?
likely_questions.purpose: Say that the Bible tells a long rescue story; do not invent a reason beyond the text.

discussion_questions.question: Who is God speaking to?
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Explain why audience matters for interpretation.

discussion_questions.question: What does the passage say will happen in the future?
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: State the wording without importing later details.

discussion_questions.question: How does later Scripture connect this hope to Christ?
What does hope look like while we still see wrongdoing?
discussion_questions.extension_prompt: Explain why hope is not pretending harm is unimportant.

activities.title: Promise Thread
steps: Add one later promise or victory card at a time.
Name the thread: evil will not win forever.
activities.learning_link: Builds a canonical connection while keeping each passage distinct.
activities.low_resource_alternative: Draw a line on the board and write references along it.

activities.title: Tangled and Untangled
steps: Name what cannot be fixed by pretending.
Connect patient repair with hope, not with a claim that every problem is easy.
activities.learning_link: Provides a concrete image for promise and patient hope.
activities.low_resource_alternative: Use a simple drawn tangle and path.

closing.prayer_prompt: Thank God that evil does not have the final word.
closing.take_home_line: God judges evil and promises rescue; evil will not win forever.

family.title: A Promise That Grows Clearer
family.parent_intro: This study introduces the Bible’s rescue thread without forcing every later detail into Genesis 3:15.

flow.instructions: Use the opening prompt to connect the lesson to ordinary family life.
Ask what Genesis says directly and what Romans adds later.
Lay down a piece of string. Put “Promise” at one end and “Victory” at the other; explain the connection in one sentence.
Choose the weekly action, then pray together.

questions: What does God promise about the serpent’s final victory?
Why should we distinguish the first promise from later explanations?

interactive.title: Promise Thread
interactive.instructions: Place two labels along a string and state what each passage contributes.

family.weekly_action: When something is wrong this week, name it honestly and choose one hopeful, faithful action.
family.prayer: God, thank You that evil will not win forever. Help us trust Jesus and keep doing what is right.
family.parent_note: Avoid telling children that every present problem will end quickly; biblical hope can involve waiting.

quiz.question: Who is addressed in Genesis 3:14-15?
quiz.explanation: The judgment speech is directed to the serpent.

quiz.question: Genesis 3:15 gives every detail of Jesus’ life, death, and resurrection.
quiz.explanation: The verse begins a promise thread but does not state every later detail.

quiz.question: What two ideas belong together in this lesson?
quiz.explanation: God addresses evil and announces future defeat.

quiz.question: What is a faithful response to God’s promise?
quiz.explanation: Hope takes wrongdoing seriously and trusts God’s victory.

puzzle.title: Text or Later Connection?
puzzle.instructions: Match each statement to Genesis 3:15 or Later Scripture.
items: Jesus defeats the power of evil.

pairs.prompt: Jesus defeats the power of evil.

printables.title: Promise Thread Card
printables.purpose: Help children distinguish Genesis 3:15 from later passages that develop the rescue promise.

accessibility.reading_level: Short concrete sentences suitable for teacher-led reading with ages 4-8.
accessibility.plain_language_rule: Use concrete verbs and define every abstract term through the story.
neurodiversity_supports: Allow pointing, drawing, or one-word responses.
Give one direction at a time.
sensory_notes: Participation must not require loud noise, touch, or public performance.
non_reader_support: Use pictures, objects, or gesture-supported retelling.

do_not_ask: Do not ask children to describe frightening experiences.
Do not use graphic injury imagery.
safeguarding.teacher_response: Use calm, non-graphic language and centre the lesson on honest hope.
